pieces.title: A physician who replaced the emperor with a constitution: Sun Yat-sen
pieces.hook: Make the goal clear, then keep organizing people around it: he practiced medicine, petitioned, rose in revolt, and built a party. The path changed; the aim of a republic…
pieces.takeaway: Make the goal clear, then keep organizing people around it: he practiced medicine, petitioned, rose in revolt, and built a party. The path changed; the aim of a republic did not.

parts: Sun Yat-sen (personal name Wen, 1866–1925) was a modern Chinese revolutionary. Today is the 160th anniversary of his birth: on November 12, 1866, he was born into a farming family in Cuiheng Village, Xiangshan County, Guangdong (today's Zhongshan).

paras.lead: Study overseas, then train as a doctor
parts: In 1879, at thirteen, he went to Honolulu with his mother and studied at Iolani School and Oahu College. After returning in 1883, a dispute over damage to a village temple statue led him to Hong Kong. From 1886 to 1892 he studied medicine in Guangzhou and Hong Kong, graduated from the Hong Kong College of Medicine, and then practiced in Macao and Guangzhou.

paras.lead: A petition fails, and he turns to revolution
parts: In 1894 he wrote to Li Hongzhang, urging reform through talent and a solid foundation for the country; the letter was not taken up. On November 24 of that year, in Honolulu, he joined more than twenty overseas Chinese to found the Xingzhonghui (Revive China Society), calling for “expelling the Tartars, restoring China, and establishing a republican government.”
In 1895 a planned uprising in Guangzhou failed before it could be launched, and he went into exile.

On October 11, 1896, he was detained at the Qing legation in London, to be smuggled back to China. His teacher James Cantlie and others campaigned for his release; the British government intervened, and he was freed on October 23, after twelve days.
The episode made him internationally famous, and turned the Qing court's pursuit into public news.

paras.lead: The Tongmenghui and the Three Principles of the People
parts: On August 20, 1905, the Xingzhonghui, the Huaxinghui and other groups formed the Tongmenghui (Chinese Revolutionary Alliance) in Tokyo. He was chosen as its head, with the oath “expel the Tartars, restore China, establish a republic, and equalize land rights.” On November 26, Min Bao was founded; in its inaugural statement he set out the three principles of nationalism, democracy, and the people's livelihood.
From then until the Huanghuagang uprising of 1911, repeated armed revolts failed.

paras.lead: The victory he was not there to see
parts: When the Wuchang Uprising broke out on October 10, 1911, he was fundraising in the United States. After province after province declared independence, he took office in Nanjing on January 1, 1912, as provisional president of the Republic of China. The Qing emperor abdicated on February 12.

To bring North and South together, he tendered his resignation to the senate on February 13 and recommended Yuan Shikai; he formally left office on April 1, after about three months. The Provisional Constitution of the Republic of China was promulgated on March 11.

Yuan later declared himself emperor, and the republican gains were eaten away. Sun launched a Second Revolution, failed, and fled to Japan; in 1914 he formed the Chinese Revolutionary Party. After 1917 he several times set up a government in Guangzhou to defend the constitution; in 1922 Chen Jiongming's troops shelled the presidential palace, and he had to flee again.

In 1924 the Kuomintang held its First National Congress, adopted an alliance with Soviet Russia and a policy of admitting Communists, and founded the Whampoa Military Academy. He hoped to use a party, an army, and propaganda to make the revolution a working organization.

paras.lead: The journey north, and the last words
parts: In November 1924 he was invited north to discuss national affairs. He died in Beijing on March 12, 1925, at the age of 58; the usual diagnosis at the time was liver cancer. The line most often quoted from his last words is “The revolution has not yet succeeded; comrades must still work hard.”

The Kuomintang honors him as Father of the Nation; the Chinese Communist Party calls him a pioneer of the democratic revolution. Critics point to the high cost of repeated uprisings, the haste of the handover to Yuan Shikai, and the way the late alliance with Russia and the Communists changed the movement's balance of power. The merits and the faults are both written into those thirty years; neither cancels the other.

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: Sun Yat-sen and the revolutionaries｜View: China could not become a modern country without overthrowing the monarchy.；Interest: Found a republic, and win overseas funds and support.；Worry: Failed uprisings, lost comrades, and scattered strength.；Basis: The Xingzhonghui, the Tongmenghui, and repeated revolts; Min Bao set out the Three Principles of the People.

The Qing court｜View: Revolution is rebellion and must be hunted down.；Interest: Keep the throne and its rule.；Worry: Overseas propaganda and armed risings would spread.；Basis: The detention at the London legation; the suppression of uprisings.

Constitutionalists and reformers｜View: Reform is safer than violence.；Interest: Widen participation inside the existing system.；Worry: Revolution would bring division and bloodshed.；Basis: He parted earlier from the reform path; Min Bao debated the constitutional press.

Yuan Shikai and the Beiyang forces｜View: Unification depends on holding the army and the center.；Interest: Take over the government.；Worry: The revolutionaries would refuse to give up power.；Basis: Sun's resignation; the later failure of the Second Revolution.

Soviet Russia and rival parties at home｜View: Organizational methods could complete a national revolution.；Interest: Widen influence in China, or grow stronger through a new alliance.；Worry: Cooperation would change the party's character.；Basis: The 1924 alliance with Russia, admission of Communists, and the founding of Whampoa; later camps have long read this choice differently.

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: The resignation bought a formal unification, and handed real power to a man more skilled at political maneuver.
Overseas Chinese supplied money; secret societies and New Army units at home supplied force. Their aims did not always match.
The alliance with Russia and the Communists strengthened organization, and also planted the seeds of a later split.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: He turned the monarchy into the name of a republic; turning that name into a stable system was harder than an uprising, and he did not live to see it.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: Recollections of how early uprisings were decided often disagree.
Liver cancer is the most common account of his last illness; later retellings do not match in every detail.
Honorifics such as “Father of the Nation” were later political names, and should not be treated as what everyone called him at the time.

pieces.title: From handwritten court gazettes to a million copies: four hundred years of the newspaper
pieces.hook: Today, news can be scrolled at any moment.

parts: Today, news can be scrolled at any moment. Four hundred years ago, printing reports of battles, sailings, and prices on a fixed schedule, putting them into strangers' hands, and getting people to pay — that itself was an invention.

China long had official documents that reported court business to the provinces, later often called dibao; in the Song there were also unofficial “small papers,” “written on small sheets and flown near and far.” They were forerunners of news, but not yet the modern newspaper: a regularly printed sheet, under a fixed title, sold to unspecified readers.
Records such as the Tang “Kaiyuan Miscellany” are still debated by scholars.

After movable type spread in Europe, single-sheet war reports and yearbooks multiplied. From 1605, Johann Carolus printed the Relation in Strasbourg, gathering current affairs at regular intervals; press historians usually treat it as the first modern newspaper.

In 1609 another German paper appeared in Wolfenbüttel. In 1650 Leipzig produced what is often called the world's first daily. In 1665 the English Oxford Gazette appeared, later the London Gazette, in a format closer to the newspaper later readers would recognize.

Early papers were often tied down by licenses and censors, copying foreign news and market prices more readily than domestic politics. Around 1695, English press licensing eased and London papers multiplied. In 1690 Benjamin Harris published Publick Occurrences in Boston; it lasted one issue before being banned. Only in 1704 did the Boston News-Letter become a paper that kept publishing in North America.

paras.lead: The steam engine brings the price down
parts: In 1785 London's Daily Universal Register was founded; three years later it was renamed The Times. In 1814 it used a steam-powered press that could print about 1,100 sheets an hour, and later could print on both sides. In the 1830s the United States saw penny papers, and France saw cheap dailies funded by advertising.

Newspapers were no longer only for gentlemen; they were sold to a much wider city readership. By the 1850s The Times sold about 40,000 copies a day and held a large share of the British daily market; in the 1890s Lloyd's Weekly Newspaper became one of the first weeklies to sell more than a million copies in a single issue.

paras.lead: Shen Bao and the modern Chinese press
parts: On April 30, 1872, the British merchant Ernest Major founded Shen Bao in Shanghai. After Shi Liangcai took it over in 1912, it gradually became one of China's most influential newspapers, until it ceased publication in May 1949. In the Shanghai area people even called a newspaper “Shenbao paper.”
Meanwhile, political reviews, commercial papers, and later party papers formed different traditions in Chinese journalism.

the paper remains, the readers have left】In the mid-twentieth century, some mass papers reached historic peaks in a single issue — the British News of the World, for example, once sold about 8 million copies in 1950. After television and the internet arrived, print circulation fell for a long stretch, and advertising moved to search, short video, and social platforms.

Many century-old papers have shrunk their print runs, gone digital-first, or kept only a website. The newspaper as “news printed on paper and sold by the day” has passed its peak. The craft of checking, editing, and reporting in public has not.

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: Publishers and newspaper houses｜View: News can be sold on a schedule, and advertising can subsidize the cover price.；Interest: Circulation, advertising revenue, and influence.；Worry: Censorship, libel suits, and costs rising faster than the sale price.；Basis: Cheap dailies were carried by ads; Shi Liangcai built Shen Bao into a major paper.

Readers｜View: They want to know what is happening outside, as cheaply and quickly as possible.；Interest: Market news, political news, and public argument.；Worry: False reports, bias, and being pulled along by emotion.；Basis: The penny press widened the audience; many people today no longer pay for a paper copy.

Governments and censors｜View: Newspapers can mobilize opinion and must be managed.；Interest: Protect order and their own image.；Worry: Criticism will spread, and secrets will leak.；Basis: Early licensing and censorship; Publick Occurrences lasted only one issue.

Reporters and editors｜View: Independent checking is the reason a newspaper exists.；Interest: Professional reputation and a steady living.；Worry: Commercial and political pressure will damage editorial independence.；Basis: Modern papers gradually formed practices of reporting, corrections, and bylines.

Internet platforms｜View: News should be instant, free, and recommendable.；Interest: Traffic and advertising.；Worry: Few people will pay for original reporting.；Basis: Print circulation and classified ads have drained away; platforms have become the main doorway.

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: Advertising made newspapers cheaper, and also made newsrooms easier to pull by advertisers and by traffic.
Governments want control; readers want to be informed. Those two lines have been in tension since the first newspaper.
Platforms have taken distribution and advertising, and often do not bear the matching cost of verification.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: The peak of the printed newspaper has passed; whether public information should still center on “edited facts” has not been settled automatically by new forms.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: What counts as “the first newspaper” depends on the definition; 1605 is the most widely shared view, not the only one.
The claim that The Times held about four-fifths of the daily market in the 1850s is an estimate of that market.
Recent exact circulation totals are counted differently from country to country; this piece does not list unverified latest figures.

pieces.title: Revenue jumped 168 percent in a year — and it still lost $700 million: CoreWeave's books
pieces.hook: After the U.S. close on November 10, the AI cloud firm CoreWeave reported third-quarter results: revenue of $3.661 billion, up 168 percent — and a net loss of $709 million.
pieces.event: After the U.S. close on 2026-11-10, third-quarter results were released; the stock closed up 24.71% on 11-11

parts: After the U.S. market close on November 10, the AI cloud company CoreWeave (Nasdaq: CRWV) reported results for the third quarter ended September 30: revenue of $3.661 billion, up 168 percent year on year — and a net loss of $709 million. The next day (November 11) the shares closed up 24.71 percent, at $60.77.

CoreWeave is based in Livingston, New Jersey. It rents out computing power built to run AI models — what the industry calls an “AI cloud” or a GPU cloud. It typically locks in customers with contracts, then borrows money to buy chips, build halls, and hook up power.

paras.lead: Revenue is rising; interest is higher still
parts: Operating income was $207 million, a 6 percent margin. Net interest expense in the same quarter was $846 million, more than wiping out that operating profit: the net loss was $709 million, or $1.27 a share. In other words, selling compute has started to make an operating profit, but the interest on money borrowed to buy the equipment still exceeds that profit.

As of September 30, the company said its revenue backlog was about $132.5 billion; CNBC, citing the firm, put the end-of-June figure at about $104 billion. It raised full-year 2026 revenue guidance to $13.0 billion–$13.3 billion, and adjusted operating income guidance to $1.275 billion–$1.375 billion.

Full-year capital-expenditure guidance was set at $37 billion–$39 billion, with the low end raised from $35 billion. The company also expects an annualized revenue run rate of $20 billion–$21 billion by year-end.

Chief executive Michael Intrator said growth is backed by several sources of funding, including loans secured by customer contracts, operating cash flow, and about $9 billion of customer prepayments and deposits expected in the next three months. At the same time, the company expects net interest expense in the fourth quarter to rise to $1.05 billion–$1.15 billion, another step up from the third quarter.

paras.lead: The power is still being laid on
parts: The company said more than 1.7 gigawatts of power is already active, roughly double the level at the start of the year, with a full-year target of more than 1.85 gigawatts; contracted power exceeds 4.6 gigawatts. The meaning is plain: contracts already run a long way ahead, while halls and power hookups are still catching up.

One backdrop is how far the stock had already fallen: on November 10 CNBC reported that in the month or so before the results, the shares were down more than 40 percent. The market's worry was not orders, but the cost of funding and the debt; some bond yields had recently topped 16 percent. Revenue that beat expectations, raised guidance, and the prepayment plan eased some of those fears.
Even after the rally, the stock was still far below its 52-week high of $138.25. That is a description of a move that has already happened, not a view of where the shares go next.

The revenue, loss, guidance, and power figures above all come from the company's November 10 release; the closing price comes from Motley Fool's market data that day. Claims that “prepayments will cover the build-out” or that “the debt risk has been cleared” are market inferences, not conclusions the company has established.
Fourth-quarter interest guidance is higher than the third quarter, which shows that financing costs are still moving forward on the books.

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: The company and its management｜View: Demand is still strong, and contracts, prepayments, and operating cash can fund further expansion.；Interest: Lock in customers, finish contracted halls, and raise full-year guidance.；Worry: Interest will keep rising, and power and delivery will lag the contracts.；Basis: The November 10 release: revenue up 168 percent year on year, a backlog of about $132.5 billion; the chief executive spoke of about $9 billion in prepayments and deposits over the next three months.

Existing shareholders and buyers｜View: Results and guidance that beat expectations justify taking back some of the recent decline.；Interest: A rebound in the shares, and confidence that the firm can keep financing itself.；Worry: Even after the bounce, the stock is still far below its high for the year, and next quarter's interest will be higher still.；Basis: On November 11 the shares closed up 24.71 percent at $60.77, still below the 52-week high of $138.25 (Motley Fool).

Bondholders and lenders｜View: They need to see whether prepayments and operating profit can support interest that is still climbing.；Interest: Collect interest on time, and reduce refinancing risk.；Worry: Bond yields are already high; if the funding window tightens again, rolling the debt will cost more.；Basis: CNBC reported that some bond yields had recently topped 16 percent; the company expects fourth-quarter net interest expense of $1.05 billion–$1.15 billion.

Customers (AI labs and cloud firms)｜View: Compute is still scarce; prepaying can lock in racks and power.；Interest: Secure deliverable training and inference capacity.；Worry: If they themselves must raise capital, a prepayment may only move money around the same chain.；Basis: The release listed continuing customers, including OpenAI, Cohere, and Perplexity; the prepayment figure comes from management.

Suppliers of chips, buildings, and power｜View: A higher capital-expenditure guide means more orders for equipment and power.；Interest: Turn the contracted 4.6 gigawatts of power and the hall projects into revenue.；Worry: Projects will slip, power will not be connected, or customers will cut spending.；Basis: The company raised the low end of full-year capital-expenditure guidance to $37 billion–$39 billion; more than 1.7 gigawatts is already active, and contracted power exceeds 4.6 gigawatts.

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: Contracts and prepayments let the company keep borrowing to expand, and also lock years of future revenue into high-interest assets.
Investors applaud that “demand is still there”; creditors watch whether interest will stay above profits.
Customer prepayments can ease the cash squeeze in front of the company, but if those customers are themselves expanding on borrowed money, the chain is still tied together.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: On the demand side the order book is already large; the constraint has moved to money and power: fourth-quarter interest guidance is still rising, and contracted power far exceeds what is already active.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: The backlog of about $132.5 billion includes contracts that have not yet met delivery conditions; it is not revenue already booked.
The end-of-June backlog of about $104 billion comes from a CNBC citation, not from a comparison stated in the full text of this release.
Bond yields “above 16 percent” are a recent level reported in the press; different notes and trading dates may differ.

pieces.title: After eight days of counting: Mississippi elects its first Black U.S. senator since Reconstruction
pieces.short: Mississippi's first Black senator since Reconstruction
pieces.hook: On November 11, the Associated Press called the race: Democrat Scott Colom had defeated Republican Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith in Mississippi.
pieces.event: 2026-11-11 (U.S. Eastern): the Associated Press called the race

parts: On November 11, the Associated Press announced that Democrat Scott Colom had defeated Republican Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, who was seeking re-election, in Mississippi's U.S. Senate race. Election Day was November 3; it took eight days before the result was called.

According to The Guardian, citing Associated Press tallies, Colom received 473,336 votes (49.2 percent), Hyde-Smith 468,667 (48.7 percent), and independent Ty Pinkins 20,234 (2.1 percent), with all precincts reported. The margin was 4,669 votes.
The AP said that after the last election-night update, Colom led by only 43 votes; the gap widened after counties finished counting absentee and provisional ballots.

This is the first time since Reconstruction that Mississippi has elected a Black U.S. senator. Senators in the Reconstruction era were chosen by the state legislature, so he is also the first Black U.S. senator from the state chosen directly by voters. The last Democrat elected to the Senate from Mississippi was John C. Stennis, in 1982.
Mississippi has the highest share of Black residents of any U.S. state.

Colom is 43 and the district attorney for the 16th Circuit. In 2015 he unseated a predecessor who had held the office for nearly thirty years, becoming the circuit's first Black district attorney. President Biden nominated him to be a federal judge in the Northern District of Mississippi, but Hyde-Smith blocked the nomination from a confirmation hearing.
On Election Day she told supporters, “I blocked Scott Colom from being a federal judge, and you blocked him from being a U.S. senator.”

On November 11, at Tougaloo College, Colom told several hundred supporters, “All I did was have the courage to imagine a night like this… I had the courage to believe in Mississippi.” Hyde-Smith then posted a concession video of about two minutes: “While this is not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters.
”Mississippi has no automatic recount; a recount can be ordered only by a court after a lawsuit.

Several outlets treated the result as another midterm blow to the Trump administration. The Guardian wrote that, with this seat, Democrats will hold at least 55 seats in the Senate, and called it the party's largest midterm gain since 1986.
That summary comes from the reporting, not from a final official roll of the Senate; if counts in other states are still not fully settled, the total may yet change.

paras.lead: The news, and a reading of it
parts: The core of the story is the count and the historical first: a seat long held by Republicans changed parties by a very narrow margin. On a reading of the numbers, the gap was only about half a percentage point, which does not suggest that the state's underlying partisan balance has flipped as a whole. As for how this will affect next year's Senate agenda, all that can be seen so far is a change in the seat count, not a concrete legislative bargain.

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: Colom and the Democrats｜View: The win shows that Mississippi “matters too,” and that the South is not beyond contest.；Interest: Take a U.S. Senate seat, and consolidate a national midterm advantage.；Worry: The lead is only about half a percentage point; governing and running again will lack a comfortable mandate.；Basis: Colom's victory speech at Tougaloo College; The Guardian said that with this seat Democrats will hold at least 55 Senate seats.

Hyde-Smith and Mississippi Republicans｜View: They respect the voters' decision, but it is not the outcome they wanted.；Interest: Hold a seat the party has long occupied.；Worry: There is no automatic recount; challenging the result would require a lawsuit.；Basis: Hyde-Smith's concession video; The Guardian reported that a recount in the state must be ordered by a court.

Mississippi voters｜View: Candidates have to answer questions about the cost of living, and also face the state's historical identity.；Interest: Elect a senator who can represent them.；Worry: A long count and a razor-thin margin can be read as “decided by one kind of ballot.”；Basis: The AP tally showed a gap of 4,669 votes; the state has the highest Black population share in the country (AP).

Trump and national Republicans｜View: Opponents will treat a loss in a particular state as punishment for the administration.；Interest: Keep the defeat framed as a local race, not a failure of a national line.；Worry: Losing another seat in a traditionally strong state would weaken their hand in Congress.；Basis: The AP placed the result in a run of midterm blows to the Trump administration; Trump had campaigned for Hyde-Smith (The Guardian).

Both parties in the incoming Congress｜View: A change in Senate numbers will affect the arithmetic of oversight, nominations, and legislation.；Interest: Win a more favorable count for next year's agenda and leadership fights.；Worry: Calling a national seat total final before every race is settled will look worse if the number later moves.；Basis: The Guardian's “at least 55 seats” is a figure in the reporting, not the final roster of the Senate clerk.

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: The winning side stresses a historic first; the losing side stresses respect for the result. Both are arguing over what this narrow win actually represents.
National parties treat Mississippi as part of the midterm weather; voters in the state are more directly facing prices, safety, and who will speak for them.
The absence of an automatic recount shortens a procedural fight, and also leaves a side that doubts the count with fewer legal remedies.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: The historical meaning can already be written down; the political effect cannot: how far a seat won by half a percentage point will change next year's Senate legislation is not yet visible in any verifiable deal or roll-call.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: The vote totals in this piece come from Associated Press figures cited by The Guardian; certified results remain a matter for state election officials.
“At least 55 Democratic seats, the largest midterm gain since 1986” is The Guardian's summary; if other states still have uncalled races, the total may change.
Hyde-Smith's Election Day line about “you blocked him” is reported as a quotation in The Guardian.
